assistant:
The overload was on **L0 (Bus_0–Bus_1)**, one of the two branches connecting the external grid; **L1 (Bus_0–Bus_2)** stayed below its limit, peaking at 54.7%.

On **5 January**, L0 exceeded 100% for **5 quarter-hour intervals (1 h 15 min)**, peaking at **107.6%** around 19:30. On **6 January**, it exceeded the limit for **10 intervals (2 h 30 min)**, peaking at **134.1%** at 19:15 and remaining overloaded through 21:00.

The operating-point data suggest the main difference was substantially greater dependence on the external grid during the 6 January evening peak: at the respective peak snapshots, import was **221.67 MW** on 6 January versus **172.39 MW** on 5 January. Load was also higher (**339.33 MW** vs **304.63 MW**), while local generation was lower (**134.36 MW** vs **143.69 MW**). That combination is consistent with the higher and longer L0 overload.

Those totals are from **different timestamps**—19:15 on 6 January and 19:30 on 5 January—so this is a comparison of each day’s peak snapshots, not identical operating conditions. It supports the explanation, but I don’t have a tool to retrieve a formal causal attribution directly. Reactive demand was filled from the default lagging power-factor assumption of 0.95.
